title: 1,987 maternal deaths in ten years
plain_language: Across 34 hospitals over 2006-2015, 1,987 women died from pregnancy or childbirth - 5% of all deaths among women aged 15-49.
so_what: Even counting only hospital deaths, the toll is large and concentrated in the reproductive years.

title: Five in six deaths were preventable direct causes
plain_language: 83.8% of maternal deaths came from direct obstetric causes - mostly eclampsia, haemorrhage and sepsis - which good emergency care can prevent.
so_what: The biggest killers are exactly the ones emergency obstetric care is built to stop.

title: Eclampsia was the leading cause
plain_language: Eclampsia caused 34% of deaths (669 women) and was the number-one killer of women aged 15-34.
so_what: Blood-pressure care in pregnancy and quick treatment of seizures would save the most young mothers.

title: Haemorrhage rose as a cause
plain_language: Bleeding caused a quarter of deaths overall (24.6%), and its share climbed from 21% in 2006-2010 to 27% in 2011-2015.
so_what: Blood, drugs and staff to manage bleeding need to keep pace - the problem is growing, not shrinking.

title: Indirect causes are a quarter of the toll
plain_language: Anaemia (14.9%) and cardiovascular disorders (14.0%) were the main indirect causes, and cardiovascular deaths rose steeply.
so_what: Programmes fixed on obstetric emergencies can miss anaemia and heart disease, which quietly kill too.

title: Most who died were 20-34
plain_language: The median age at death was 27, and two thirds of deaths were among women aged 20-34 - the peak childbearing years.
so_what: Deaths track where births happen, so services for this age group carry the most weight.

title: Fewer teenage mothers died
plain_language: Deaths among 15-19 year olds fell from 17.8% of the total in 2006-2010 to 11.1% in 2011-2015.
so_what: One bright spot: risk to the youngest mothers eased, even as the overall rate rose.

title: The hospital death rate rose over 40%
plain_language: The hospital maternal mortality ratio climbed from 40.24 per 100,000 births in 2006 to 57.94 in 2015, peaking at 69.64 in 2011.
so_what: More women giving birth in facilities is good, but it also means facilities must be ready to save them.

title: Different ages, different killers
plain_language: Eclampsia was the top killer of young women (15-34); haemorrhage led among older women (35-49); ruptured uterus was commonest in women over 45.
so_what: Care can be tailored by age - watch blood pressure in the young, bleeding in the older.
